title: Mortgage Interest Rates: What Determines Yours and How to Get a Better One

seo.seoTitle: Mortgage Interest Rates: What Affects Yours
seo.metaDescription: Mortgage rates are shaped by the broader market and your personal financial profile. Here's exactly what moves rates, what you control, and how to secure a better one.
secondaryKeywords: how to get a lower mortgage rate
seo.searchIntent: Informational/commercial — users wanting to understand what drives their mortgage rate and how to secure the lowest one available to them

excerpt: Mortgage rates move for reasons entirely outside your control and reasons entirely within it. Here's how to tell the difference — and what actually moves the needle on the rate you're offered.
intro:
Mortgage rates are set by a combination of broad economic forces — inflation expectations, Federal Reserve policy, bond market conditions — and your individual financial profile: credit score, down payment, loan type, and debt levels. The first category is completely outside any individual borrower's control. The second is almost entirely within it, and it's where the real opportunity to secure a meaningfully better rate lives.

This guide separates the two, explains what actually moves rates broadly, and walks through the concrete steps that improve the rate a lender offers you specifically.

sections.heading: What Moves Mortgage Rates Broadly
paragraphs: Mortgage rates generally track the bond market, particularly long-term Treasury yields, and respond to inflation expectations and Federal Reserve policy signals, even though the Fed doesn't directly set mortgage rates the way it sets short-term rates. When inflation is expected to run hot, rates tend to rise; when the economic outlook weakens and rate cuts are expected, mortgage rates often ease in anticipation.

None of this is something an individual borrower can influence — but understanding it helps explain why the rate your neighbor got last year, or the rate advertised on the news, may look completely different from what you're quoted today.

sections.heading: Adjustable-Rate Mortgages and Rate Risk
paragraphs: An adjustable-rate mortgage typically offers a lower initial rate than a comparable fixed-rate loan, but that rate adjusts periodically after an introductory period based on a reference index plus a margin set by the lender. Most ARMs include caps limiting how much the rate can move at each adjustment and over the life of the loan, which bounds the worst-case scenario but doesn't eliminate the underlying risk that your payment could rise meaningfully if rates move against you.

Borrowers considering an ARM should model the maximum possible payment under the loan's cap structure, not just the attractive introductory rate, and honestly assess whether that worst-case payment would still be manageable — the lower initial rate only pays off if your plans (selling, refinancing, or comfortably absorbing a higher payment) actually play out as expected. ARM terms are often described with two numbers, such as 5/1 or 7/6, indicating the length of the initial fixed period and how frequently the rate adjusts afterward — understanding this notation is worth confirming with your loan officer before assuming you know exactly when your rate could first change.

sections.heading: What You Control: Credit Score and Debt-to-Income
paragraphs: Within the market environment on any given day, your credit score is the single largest factor lenders use to price your individual rate. Borrowers in the highest credit tiers routinely receive noticeably better rates than those in lower tiers, even on an identical loan amount and property.

Your debt-to-income ratio (DTI) — total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income — also matters significantly. A lower DTI signals more capacity to absorb the new mortgage payment and typically supports a better rate and easier approval.

callout.title: Check your credit report before applying
callout.text: Pull your credit reports and dispute any errors well before you apply. A single incorrect late payment or an outdated balance can meaningfully lower your score and the rate you're offered.

sections.heading: Loan Type, Term, and Down Payment
paragraphs: Shorter loan terms (15-year vs 30-year) typically carry lower rates in exchange for a higher monthly payment. A larger down payment can also improve your rate, both by reducing the lender's risk and, on conventional loans, by helping you avoid or reduce private mortgage insurance. Government-backed loan types (FHA, VA, USDA) have their own rate and insurance structures that can be more or less favorable depending on your specific financial profile — see [the complete guide to mortgages](/financial-intelligence/complete-guide-to-mortgages) for how each type compares.

sections.heading: Mortgage Points: Buying Down Your Rate
paragraphs: Discount points let you pay an upfront fee at closing in exchange for a lower interest rate for the life of the loan. Each point typically costs a percentage of the loan amount and reduces the rate by a modest fixed amount, though the exact math varies by lender.

Whether points make sense depends entirely on how long you plan to keep the loan: the upfront cost needs enough time to be recovered through the lower monthly payment before it's worth it. If you expect to sell or refinance within a few years, paying for points rarely pays off; if you're confident you'll hold the loan long-term, it often does.

sections.heading: Interest Rate vs APR
paragraphs: The interest rate reflects only the cost of borrowing the principal. The Annual Percentage Rate (APR) rolls in the interest rate plus most lender fees and closing costs, expressed as a yearly rate — making it the more accurate number for comparing loan offers from different lenders, since a lower rate with high fees can have a higher APR than a slightly higher rate with minimal fees.

sections.heading: Rate Locks: Protecting Your Rate Before Closing
paragraphs: Once you've chosen a lender and rate, a rate lock guarantees that specific rate for a set period — commonly 30 to 60 days — protecting you from rate increases while your loan moves through underwriting to closing. If rates fall after you lock, some lenders offer a one-time 'float down' option to capture a portion of the improvement, though this varies by lender and often carries a fee.

Locking too early, before you're confident the closing timeline will hold, risks the lock expiring before closing, which can require an extension (sometimes at a cost) or re-locking at a potentially less favorable current rate. Coordinate the lock timing with your loan officer once your closing date is reasonably firm, and ask specifically what the extension policy and cost look like before you lock, so there are no surprises if the closing timeline shifts for reasons outside your control. Some lenders also offer a longer initial lock period for a modest fee, which can be worth considering if you expect the closing process to take longer than the standard 30 to 60 days, particularly for new construction or a more complex transaction. Ask your loan officer to walk through the specific lock terms in writing rather than relying on a verbal summary, since the fee structure for extensions and float-downs varies enough between lenders that assumptions carried over from a previous mortgage may not apply this time. Getting the specifics in writing also protects you if a disagreement arises later about what was actually promised at the time of the lock, which matters more than it might seem given how much money a rate difference can represent over a 30-year term.

sections.heading: How to Actually Get a Lower Rate
paragraphs: Improve your credit score before applying by paying down revolving balances and correcting any report errors. Save for a larger down payment where feasible. Shop multiple lenders — rate quotes for the same borrower can vary meaningfully between lenders on the same day, and getting several quotes within a short window typically counts as a single credit inquiry for scoring purposes. Compare APR, not just the headline rate, and run the numbers on points if you're confident about your timeline.

Rates are also worth revisiting after closing: if market rates drop meaningfully after you've locked in, [refinancing a mortgage](/financial-intelligence/refinancing-a-mortgage) can capture the savings, provided the refinance costs are outweighed by the new rate's benefit over your remaining time in the home.

keyTakeaways: Mortgage rates move broadly with the bond market, inflation expectations, and Fed policy — none of which an individual borrower controls.
Your credit score and debt-to-income ratio are the biggest levers you do control when it comes to the rate you're personally offered.
Shorter loan terms and larger down payments generally support lower rates and can reduce or avoid mortgage insurance.
Mortgage points trade an upfront fee for a lower rate — worth it mainly if you're confident you'll hold the loan long enough to recoup the cost.
Compare APR, not just the interest rate, since APR includes fees and gives the true cost of a loan offer.
Shopping multiple lenders within a short window typically counts as one credit inquiry and can meaningfully change the rate you're offered.

faq.question: What is a good mortgage interest rate?
faq.answer: "Good" is relative to current market conditions at the time you're borrowing — the more useful comparison is how your rate compares to other current offers for your credit profile, loan type, and term, not to rates from a different rate environment.

faq.question: Does my credit score really affect my mortgage rate that much?
faq.answer: Yes — it's typically the single largest factor within your control. Borrowers in the top credit tiers routinely receive noticeably better rates than those in lower tiers on an identical loan.

faq.question: Are mortgage points worth paying for?
faq.answer: Only if you're confident you'll hold the loan long enough for the lower monthly payment to recover the upfront cost — generally a multi-year time horizon. If you might sell or refinance soon, points usually aren't worth it.

faq.question: Should I compare interest rate or APR when shopping for a mortgage?
faq.answer: APR, since it includes most lender fees and closing costs alongside the interest rate, giving a more complete picture of the loan's true cost.

faq.question: How many lenders should I get mortgage quotes from?
faq.answer: Most guidance suggests at least three to four, since rate offers for the same borrower can vary meaningfully between lenders. Getting quotes within a focused window typically counts as a single inquiry for credit scoring purposes.

faq.question: What is a mortgage rate lock?
faq.answer: A guarantee from your lender that your quoted rate won't change for a set period, commonly 30 to 60 days, protecting you from rate increases while your loan moves through underwriting to closing.

faq.question: What happens if my rate lock expires before closing?
faq.answer: You may need to pay for an extension or re-lock at the current rate, which could be higher or lower than your original lock. Coordinating the lock timing with a realistic closing date helps avoid this.

faq.question: How risky is an adjustable-rate mortgage?
faq.answer: It depends on the rate caps and your plans — model the maximum possible payment under the loan's cap structure, not just the introductory rate, and confirm you could comfortably manage that worst-case scenario if your plans to sell or refinance change.

conclusion:
Mortgage rates are shaped by forces you can't influence and factors you absolutely can. The market-wide piece sets the baseline everyone is working with on a given day; your credit score, debt-to-income ratio, down payment, and choice of lender determine where you land relative to that baseline.

Before you lock in a rate, get your credit report in order, shop multiple lenders, compare APR rather than the headline number, and run the real math on points if you're weighing them. And once you're in the loan, keep an eye on the market — [refinancing a mortgage](/financial-intelligence/refinancing-a-mortgage) later, if conditions improve, is always an option worth revisiting.
